t: LeetCode 2063 - Vowels of All Substrings: Contribution Counting
o: **Understanding the problem.** We need the total number of vowels summed over all n(n+1)/2 substrings of word. For "aba" the substrings a, ab, aba, b, ba, a carry 1, 1, 2, 0, 1, 1 vowels respectively - total 6. For "abc" only a, ab and abc contain a vowel, giving 3, while "ltcd" gives 0. Enumerating substrings is quadratic and hopeless for n up to 100000 (roughly ten billion steps). The fix is to invert the question: instead of asking how many vowels each substring has, ask in how many substrings each individual vowel occurrence appears - a product of two independent counts.
k: Sum-over-all-substrings problems usually flip to contribution counting: process each element once, multiplied by its multiplicities.
A character at index i appears in every substring choosing a start at most i and an end at least i: exactly (i + 1) * (n - i) substrings.
The answer approaches n^3 / 6, so 64-bit accumulation is mandatory in fixed-width languages.

a.i: Fix each start and sweep the end, carrying the vowel count of the growing substring and adding it to the answer after every extension. This mirrors the statement directly but touches every start-end pair.
s: For each start i set cnt = 0.
Extend j from i to the end, incrementing cnt whenever word[j] is a vowel.
Add cnt to the answer after each extension.
a.t: O(n^2) - all substring endpoints are visited; too slow when n = 100000

a.n: Approach 2: Multiply Each Vowel by Its Reach
a.i: A vowel at index i is included by i + 1 choices of start and n - i choices of end, contributing (i + 1)(n - i) to the total. Non-vowels contribute nothing, so one additive pass finishes the problem.
s: Scan word once with a 64-bit accumulator.
When word[i] is a vowel, add (i + 1) * (n - i) to the accumulator as a wide integer.
a.t: O(n) - single pass over the string

w: Reach for the contribution technique whenever an aggregate is taken over all subarrays: multiplying each element by left-endpoint choices times right-endpoint choices collapses quadratic enumeration to linear. The main trap is overflow - totals near n cubed over six demand long long in C++ and long in Java (cast before multiplying), while Python integers and JavaScript doubles (safe below 2^53) are fine. Follow-ups: vowel sums restricted to a fixed substring length, or supporting point updates with a Fenwick tree over contributions.
